transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi. Yeah, um, thanks. I guess what brings me in is that I’m just... I'm losing hours every single day to rechecking things. It's getting really bad. Like my door locks, my dressing supplies in the bathroom, and especially work stuff—file dimensions, revision notes. 

I'm an engineer, so I'm looking at schematics all day, and we actually just switched to this new project management software last month. It's completely terrible. I told my boss the migration would mess up the legacy CAD files, and of course, it did, so now I'm spending half my week fixing formatting issues instead of doing actual design work. I didn't go to grad school to just click through drop-down menus all day, you know? My buddy Dave—he works at a different firm—he said they tried the exact same software and dropped it after a week because it kept crashing their servers. 

But anyway, sorry, the problem is that with the file dimensions, or the revision notes, or even just the locks at my apartment... I don’t feel allowed to move on to the next task until I’ve gone through the exact same checking routine enough times. Like, I have to keep doing it over and over until the anxiety finally drops. If it doesn't feel right, I'm just stuck there.
Do you ever feel like you have to check these things because something bad might happen if you don't?

Yeah, exactly. It's like... even after I know I've cleaned a wound area, or I've reviewed a CAD file for the tenth time, this thought just keeps cutting in. It's like this loud voice saying I missed one tiny thing, and because of that, it's going to turn into a massive infection, or a design mistake that actually hurts someone. And I can't just reason it away, no matter how much I know the math is right. 

Which is wild, because in engineering, everything is about reasoning things away. You have tolerances, you have safety factors. My professor in grad school, Dr. Aris, he used to hammer that into us. He'd say, "If you're designing a bridge for a hundred cars, you build it to hold a thousand." He was this old Greek guy, brilliant, but he had this weird habit of always wearing sandals to the lab, even in December. Like, full-on blizzard outside, and he's just shuffling around in Birkenstocks. We always wondered if he had some kind of circulation issue, or maybe he just didn't care. He actually got written up by the safety committee once because someone dropped a wrench near his foot. 

But yeah, the thoughts... they just don't listen to logic. I know the file is fine, but I just feel this overwhelming dread that if I don't check it one more time, something catastrophic is on my hands.
Do you feel like you have to perform these checking routines in a very specific way?

Yeah, um, exactly. It's like I was saying before about losing all those hours every day. With the door locks, or my dressing supplies, or the file dimensions... it has to be the exact same routine. I basically don't feel allowed to move on to the next thing until I’ve gone through that specific sequence enough times that the anxiety finally drops. 

Which, actually, is even more of a nightmare now because my apartment building just swapped all our deadbolts for these new smart locks. You have to use an app on your phone to lock and unlock them, and it connects via Bluetooth, which is incredibly insecure if you actually look at the encryption standards they use for these commercial models. Plus the app just completely drains your battery. My neighbor down the hall, Mrs. Gable, she stepped out to grab a package last week and her phone died, and she got locked out in her pajamas. She had to sit in the lobby for two hours waiting for the super to come let her in, and our lobby always smells like this really aggressive, cheap vanilla air freshener. I felt so bad for her, she has this little terrier that was just barking on the other side of the door the whole time. 

But um... yeah, sorry, what was I saying? Right, the checking routine. If I don't do it the exact same way, in the exact right order, I just can't stop. I have to keep repeating it until that feeling drops.
Do you feel like something bad would happen if you didn't complete these checking routines?

Yeah, I mean, kind of like I was saying a minute ago, it's just this overwhelming feeling that I'm not allowed to move on. If I don't finish checking the door locks, or the file dimensions, or my dressing supplies... I just end up losing hours to it because the anxiety won't drop until I've gone through the routine enough times. 

Actually, with the dressing supplies, I've had to start buying them in bulk from this medical supply warehouse out in the suburbs because the local pharmacy stopped carrying the exact hydrocolloid ones I need. The guy who owns the warehouse, his name is Gary, and he is absolutely obsessed with model trains. He actually built this massive track that runs along the ceiling of the store, right above all the aisles of wheelchairs and gauze. It's a really incredible setup, honestly. He custom-painted all the little boxcars to look like the Union Pacific line from the 1950s, and he was telling me how he had to 3D print custom brackets to mount the tracks because the drop ceiling couldn't support the weight. I spent like twenty minutes talking to him about the tensile strength of the filament he used last time I was in there. 

But, um, what were we talking about? Oh, right, the bad feeling. Yeah, if I don't do the checking routine enough times, I just stay stuck there. I can't move on to the next thing until the anxiety actually drops.
Do you feel like you have to think specific thoughts or repeat certain words or phrases in your head as part of your checking routines?

Um, no, not really thoughts or words in my head. It's more about the physical actions, like I was saying. I just lose hours every day to rechecking things. The dressing supplies, the door locks, the file dimensions, the revision notes... it's all physical checking. I just don't feel allowed to move on until I've gone through that same routine enough times that the anxiety drops. 

Which is why the revision notes are such a problem right now. We use this project management software at work that is just terribly designed. The UI is completely cluttered, and they recently pushed an update that changed the default font to something that looks like Comic Sans but somehow worse. My coworker, Dave, he actually submitted a formal complaint to IT about it because he said it was giving him a headache. Dave is a bit dramatic, though. He brings his own espresso machine to the office and gets really defensive if anyone else tries to use it. He even buys these imported beans from Italy that cost like forty dollars a bag. I tried one once when he was on vacation, and honestly, it just tasted burnt to me. But he swears by it. 

But yeah, um... no specific words or anything. Just the checking routines over and over until the feeling goes away.
Are you worried that if you don't check these things, someone might get hurt or something bad might happen to them?

Yeah, exactly. That's exactly it. It's like... even after I know I've cleaned the wound area perfectly, or I've reviewed a CAD file for work a dozen times, this thought just keeps cutting in. It tells me I missed one tiny thing, and that one little oversight is going to turn into a massive infection, or a catastrophic design mistake that actually hurts someone. And I can't just reason it away, no matter how much I try. 

Which is really stressful at work, especially because we just got this new contract to design the structural supports for a pedestrian bridge downtown. The city council has been arguing about this bridge for like three years. Apparently, the original proposal was for this really modern, sleek glass thing, but the historical society threw a fit because it didn't match the brick architecture of the old warehouse district. So now we're doing this hybrid steel and brick facade design, which is a nightmare for weight distribution. My project manager, Sarah, she's been so stressed about it she started bringing her cat to the office for emotional support. It's this massive Maine Coon named Barnaby, and he just sleeps on top of the server rack all day because it's warm. He shed all over my keyboard last week, and I had to use a can of compressed air to get the fur out from under the keys. 

But um... yeah, what was I saying? Right, the fear of someone getting hurt. It's just this constant thought that I missed something, and it's going to cause a disaster, and I just can't shake it.
Are your checking routines mostly about preventing harm or mistakes, or are they also about preventing contamination or germs?

Um, mostly it's just about the harm and the mistakes, like I was saying. I don't really have the germ thing. I mean, I clean the wound area, obviously, because you have to, but I'm not, like, terrified of germs everywhere else. It's just the fear of making a mistake that causes a disaster. 

Like with the CAD files, right? If I mess up a tolerance on a structural support, that's not germs, that's physics. Speaking of physics, I was watching this documentary last night about the collapse of the Tacoma Narrows Bridge. You know, the one in the 1940s that started twisting in the wind before it just completely fell apart? It's fascinating because it wasn't a structural flaw in the traditional sense, it was aeroelastic flutter. The wind matched the resonant frequency of the bridge. The original engineer, Leon Moisseiff, he was actually a really prominent bridge designer at the time, and that failure completely ruined his career. He died just a few years later, and some people say it was from a heart attack brought on by the stress of the whole thing. It's crazy to think about how one design choice can just end up defining your entire legacy like that. 

But, um, yeah. Not germs. Just mistakes. I just can't stop checking to make sure I didn't make a mistake.
Do you feel like your checking routines need to be done a specific number of times, or is it more about doing them until it feels 'right' or 'complete'?

Um, it's definitely not a specific number. It's... it's exactly what you said, doing it until it feels right. Like I was saying before, that's really what brings me in here, because I'm just losing hours every single day to rechecking things. The dressing supplies, the door locks, the file dimensions, the revision notes... I just don't feel allowed to move on until I've gone through that same routine enough times that the anxiety finally drops. 

Which is exhausting, especially with the door locks. My apartment building actually just installed these new smart locks last month, the kind you open with an app on your phone instead of a key. The landlord said it was for security, but I'm pretty sure he just wanted to stop paying a locksmith every time someone lost their keys. The app is incredibly buggy, though. Sometimes it takes like five seconds to register that you've tapped the unlock button, and you just end up standing in the hallway looking like an idiot. My neighbor across the hall, Mrs. Higgins, she refused to use it. She's like eighty years old and doesn't even own a smartphone. She actually threatened to call the housing authority until the landlord agreed to give her a physical override key. I honestly wish I had one too, because at least with a physical key, you can feel it turn. With the app, it's just this little digital chime, and I don't trust it. I have to stand there and pull on the handle over and over to make sure it actually engaged. 

But um, yeah... it's not a number. It's just until the anxiety drops and it feels like I'm allowed to stop.
Do you feel like your checking routines are also about making sure things are symmetrical or exactly right, not just about preventing harm or mistakes?

Um, no, not really. It's not about symmetry or anything like that. I don't care if things are lined up perfectly on my desk or whatever. It's really just the harm thing, making sure I didn't screw up. 

Although, speaking of my desk, I did just buy this new monitor stand because my neck was killing me from looking down all day. It's one of those adjustable bamboo ones, supposed to be really ergonomic. I ordered it from this company that plants a tree for every purchase, which is cool, I guess, but the shipping took forever. It got stuck in a distribution center in Ohio for like two weeks. I ended up calling customer service, and the guy on the phone—I think his name was Greg—he sounded so tired. He told me they've been dealing with this massive backlog because their main logistics partner went bankrupt overnight. Just totally folded. All these packages were just sitting in warehouses with nobody to move them. It makes you realize how fragile the whole supply chain is, you know? Like, one company goes under and suddenly nobody can get their bamboo monitor stands or, I don't know, medical supplies or whatever. 

But, uh, anyway. No, it's not about symmetry. Just preventing a disaster.
Do you think that if you didn't do these checking routines, the potential harm or mistakes you're trying to prevent would happen to you or to someone else?

Um, mostly to someone else, I think. Like, if I'm checking the CAD files, the fear is always that a structural support will fail and someone will get hurt because of my design mistake. And with the wound, it's... well, I guess that one is about me getting an infection, but it still feels like this huge disaster waiting to happen. 

Even after I know I've cleaned the wound area, or I've reviewed the file, this thought just keeps cutting in. It's like, what if I missed one tiny thing? And I just can't reason it away. It's so frustrating, because logically I know I did it right. 

Speaking of doing things right, my firm just hired this new junior engineer, and I'm supposed to be mentoring him. He's fresh out of grad school, super eager, but he uses this completely outdated version of AutoCAD because that's what his professor insisted on teaching. I told him he needs to update his software, but he's weirdly stubborn about it. He said his professor told him the newer versions have too much bloatware and it slows down the rendering process. Which, okay, maybe a little bit, but the integration features you lose just aren't worth it. Plus, our whole server is set up for the current version, so every time he saves a file, it creates this weird compatibility error log that the IT guy has to manually clear out. The IT guy, Dave, he is not happy about it. Dave's been with the company for like twenty years and he basically lives in the server room. He has this massive collection of vintage mechanical keyboards in there. He let me try one the other day, an old IBM Model M from the 80s. The clicking sound it makes is incredible, but it weighs like five pounds. You could probably use it as a weapon if you had to. 

But, um, what was I... right, the mistakes. Yeah, it's just this thought that I missed something tiny that's going to hurt someone or cause an infection, and I just can't shake it.
Do you think someone else could get hurt if you didn't check things as thoroughly as you do?

Yeah, absolutely. Like I just said, that's exactly what I'm afraid of with the CAD files. If I don't check them, a support could fail and someone could actually get hurt. It's always about someone else getting hurt, unless it's the wound thing, which is about me. 

But with the structural stuff, it's terrifying. Actually, there was this documentary I watched last weekend about this bridge collapse in Italy a few years ago. The Morandi Bridge, I think it was called? It was horrifying. Dozens of people died just because of, like, corrosion and lack of maintenance that nobody caught in time. The documentary went into all this detail about the original engineer, this guy Riccardo Morandi, and how his design was actually really innovative for the time, using prestressed concrete. But concrete degrades, you know? Especially with all the salt in the air near the coast. And they interviewed this one survivor who was literally driving a delivery truck across it when the road just vanished in front of him. He managed to stop like three feet from the edge. It's crazy to think about how much trust we put into infrastructure every single day without even realizing it. Like, you just drive over a bridge and assume the person who designed it checked their math. 

So, yeah... that's why I have to check. Because if I don't, I'm terrified someone will get hurt because of my mistake.
Do you feel like you're checking things to prevent mistakes or because you need to feel in control of the situation?

Um, I don't really think it's about control, exactly. It's more just... well, that's actually the main thing that brings me in here. I'm losing hours every day just rechecking things. Like my dressing supplies, the door locks at my apartment, the CAD file dimensions at work, my revision notes. I just don't feel allowed to move on to the next thing until I've gone through the exact same routine enough times that the anxiety finally drops. 

Like with the door locks, I actually checked the deadbolt on my apartment so many times last week that the internal mechanism kind of jammed up, and I had to call a locksmith. This guy showed up in this totally rusted-out van, but he had the most incredible set of tools. He was explaining to me how standard pin tumbler locks work, which, being an engineer, I found super fascinating. Apparently, most residential locks are ridiculously easy to bypass. He used this thing called a bump key and had my door open in literally ten seconds. It totally makes you wonder why we even bother locking our doors if anyone can just buy a bump key on the internet and get in. He told me he actually learned how to pick locks from watching YouTube videos, which is kind of wild for a professional locksmith, right? He was saying he wants to start his own channel where he just reviews different padlock brands and rates their security flaws. He even had this custom camera mount he 3D printed for his phone so he could film close-ups of the keyholes without his hands shaking. 

But, um, anyway. Yeah. It's not really about feeling like I'm the one in control of the situation. It's just that I have to do the checking routine until that horrible anxious feeling goes away so I can finally move on with my day.
Do you believe that if you didn't perform these checking routines, your mistakes could lead to severe consequences, such as injury or death?

Yeah, I mean... I think I kind of just said that, didn't I? Like with the CAD files, definitely injury. And yeah, death too, if a structure actually collapsed because of a load-bearing miscalculation. It's a massive liability. 

Actually, we just had this huge mandatory seminar on professional liability and catastrophic failures at work last month. They brought in this guest speaker from an insurance firm in Chicago. He was this really intense guy who kept pacing back and forth across the conference room, and he was wearing these incredibly shiny wingtip shoes. Like, they were so polished they were literally reflecting the overhead fluorescent lights right into my eyes. I was trying to focus on his presentation, but they had catered lunch from this local deli, and they completely messed up the order. They brought like thirty egg salad sandwiches and nothing else. Who orders just egg salad for a room full of engineers? Half the office wouldn't even touch them, so they just sat there on the conference table getting warm. My coworker, Ben, he ate like three of them anyway and then complained about stomach cramps the rest of the afternoon. Ben is always doing stuff like that, though. He has zero impulse control when it comes to free food. He once ate a whole box of stale donuts that had been sitting in the breakroom over a long weekend. 

But, um, what were you asking? Oh, right, the severe consequences. Yeah. I do believe that. If I don't check my work, something fatal could happen, and I just can't let that happen.
Do you feel personally responsible for preventing harm to others through your checking routines?

I mean, I don't know if I'd use the exact words 'personally responsible'... but yeah, I guess? If it's my CAD file, my name is on it, so it's on me to make sure it's right. My name is actually on a lot of extra projects right now because we're really understaffed. 

Our senior project manager, Dave, just went on paternity leave. He and his wife just had twins, which is totally crazy. I can't even imagine having one kid, let alone two at the exact same time. They named them Liam and Lucas. Dave was showing us pictures on his phone in the breakroom right before he left, and honestly, they just looked like little wrinkly red potatoes. I didn't say that to him, obviously, I just smiled and said 'oh wow, congratulations' like you're supposed to. But newborn babies are just so weird looking. They have those razor-sharp tiny little fingernails. My sister had a baby last year, and she had to buy these special little cotton mittens for him so he wouldn't scratch his own face up while he was sleeping. I didn't even know baby mittens were a thing before that. They're so incredibly small, they look like they belong on a doll or something. 

But, um... wait, what were you asking? Oh, about being responsible. I don't know, I'm not really sure how to answer that. I just... I just know if I don't do my checks, and something goes wrong, it's my fault.
Do you feel like your checking is a way to protect others from potential harm that you might cause?

Yeah, I suppose it is about protecting them. Because even after I know I've completely cleaned the wound area—I got this nasty scrape last week—or after I've reviewed a CAD file... 

Actually, I got the scrape working on my mountain bike. I bought it off Craigslist from this guy who lived way out in the suburbs, and he had like, six cats just roaming around his garage. It smelled so strongly of ammonia in there, I could barely breathe. One of the cats actually jumped onto his workbench while I was looking at the suspension and knocked over a whole open tin of chain grease. It got all over my shoes. I was wearing my favorite sneakers, these gray New Balances. You can't even get them anymore because the factory stopped producing that specific colorway. I tried using Dawn dish soap to get the stain out, because they always use that on ducks in oil spills in those commercials, right? But it really only works well on, like, plastic Tupperware. Which reminds me, my roommate keeps taking my good glass meal-prep containers to work and just leaving them in his office fridge until things literally grow in them. It's so gross. I had to throw away a really nice lid the other day because it was stained orange from spaghetti sauce. 

But, um... anyway, what was I saying? The checking. Right. The thing is, even when I know for a fact I've cleaned the wound perfectly, or I've checked the CAD file a dozen times, this thought just keeps cutting in. It just tells me that I missed one tiny thing, and because of that, it's going to turn into a horrible infection, or a design mistake that ends up hurting someone. And I just can't reason it away. No matter how much logic I try to use, the thought just stays there until I check it again.
Do you feel like your checking routines are a way to avoid feeling guilty if something bad were to happen to someone else because of your potential mistake?

Guilt? I don't... I mean, I'm not really sure if it's about avoiding guilt. I haven't really thought about it that way. I do feel guilty about other things, though. Like, last week I accidentally knocked over my roommate's houseplant and broke the pot. It was this really nice ceramic one he got at a farmer's market. 

The farmer's market downtown is actually getting huge, they shut down like four blocks of Main Street for it now on Saturday mornings. I went a couple of weeks ago to get some local honey because someone told me it helps with seasonal allergies. I don't even know if that's scientifically true, but the honey guy there had this crazy setup with a live observation hive right on his table. You could see all the bees crawling around inside this glass case. It was kind of mesmerizing, honestly, but also a little freaky because what if the glass broke? There were so many little kids running around, too. This one kid with a bright red balloon kept bumping into the table, and the mom wasn't even paying attention, she was just arguing with someone on her cell phone about a timeshare in Florida. Timeshares are such a massive scam anyway, my uncle got trapped in one in Orlando for like ten years and he could never even book the weeks he wanted... 

But, um... sorry, I completely lost my train of thought. What were we talking about? Oh, right, the guilt thing. Yeah, I don't really know if guilt is the right word for it. I just don't want anyone to get hurt, so I check.
Do you believe your checking routines are a way to prevent yourself from feeling responsible if something bad happens to someone else because of a potential mistake you made?

I mean, maybe? It's not so much about the feeling of responsibility, it's just... I can't stop. What brings me in is that I'm losing hours to rechecking things. Like my dressing supplies for that scrape, the door locks, file dimensions at work, revision notes... I just don't feel allowed to move on until I've gone through the same routine enough times that the anxiety drops. 

Speaking of door locks, my apartment building just installed these new smart locks on all the exterior doors. You have to use an app on your phone to get in now, which is so annoying if your battery dies. And my phone battery is always dying because I have this older iPhone. Apple totally throttles the batteries on older models to force you to upgrade, I swear. I was reading this huge thread on Reddit about it the other night when I couldn't sleep. There's this whole community of people who refuse to upgrade and they just keep replacing the batteries themselves using these tiny little screwdrivers you can buy online. I actually ordered a kit, but when it arrived, the screwdrivers were magnetized, which is supposedly really bad for the logic board. I don't know if that's true, but I didn't want to risk bricking my phone. My buddy Steve bricked his phone once trying to jailbreak it so he could get free games, and he had to go to the Apple Store and pretend he didn't know what happened. The Genius Bar guy totally knew, though. They always know. 

But, uh... wait. What did you ask me? Oh, right, about preventing myself from feeling responsible. I don't know, I just... I just have to do the routine until the anxiety goes away. That's the only way I can explain it.
Do you think your checking routines are a way to cope with the fear of being responsible if someone gets hurt because of one of your mistakes?

I don't think it's about coping with the fear of being responsible, really. I just... I don't know, I just don't want anyone to get hurt, so I check. It's not like a conscious thought of "oh, I'll be blamed for this." It's more just this overwhelming feeling that I have to do it. 

Like when I was checking the CAD files yesterday. I had to go through every single layer, even the ones that were just reference lines. Which is so tedious because the software we use is incredibly slow. We're still using this ancient version of AutoCAD from like 2018 because the company doesn't want to pay for the subscription model. They switched to that a few years ago and it made everyone so mad. My boss, Dave, he actually wrote this huge, angry email to their customer support, as if that was going to change their entire corporate business model. Dave is always doing stuff like that. He got into a screaming match with the barista at Starbucks last week because they put whole milk in his latte instead of oat milk. He's super lactose intolerant, to be fair, but still. You don't have to yell at a teenager making minimum wage. I always tip them extra when he does that. I usually use the app to tip, though, because who carries cash anymore? I tried to use a twenty-dollar bill at a food truck the other day and the guy looked at me like I handed him a live grenade. He had this little Square reader plugged into his iPad, but the screen was completely shattered. I don't know how he could even read the orders...

Sorry, I'm doing it again. What was the question? Something about coping with fear? Yeah, I don't really know. I just check because I have to.
Do you think your checking routines are mostly about avoiding the feeling of being at fault if something bad happens to someone else?

At fault? I mean, I'm not really thinking about who gets the blame, honestly. I just don't want anything bad to happen. 

Speaking of being at fault, though, my car insurance premium just went up even though I totally wasn't at fault for this fender bender I had last month. This guy in a Prius just backed right into me in the grocery store parking lot. It was the Trader Joe's over on 5th, and their parking lot is an absolute nightmare. They always build them way too small on purpose, I swear. My buddy works in urban planning and he says it's a known psychological trick to make the store seem more exclusive or busy, which is just brilliant but so annoying when you're just trying to buy some frozen potstickers. 

But anyway, the guy tried to say I was in his blind spot. Which is ridiculous because I was completely stationary. Thank god I had a dashcam installed. I bought this really nice Garmin one off Amazon during Prime Day last year. Prime Day deals used to be so good, but now it's just a bunch of cheap drop-shipped electronics with weird brand names in all caps. You really have to use those price tracker extensions on your browser to see if you're actually getting a deal, otherwise they just mark up the base price and pretend it's on sale. I actually wrote a little Python script to track prices for me, since it's easier than relying on third-party extensions that probably just sell your data anyway. Data privacy is basically dead at this point, every single app tracks your location even when you tell it not to...

Wait, sorry. I'm rambling again. What did you ask me? About being at fault? Yeah, I don't really think about the blame part of it. I just get stuck doing the checks until my brain finally lets me move on.
Do you believe that your checking routines are a way to prevent yourself from feeling responsible if something bad were to happen to someone else?

I don't think it's about preventing myself from feeling responsible. I'm not really sitting there thinking about the consequences like that. It's just... I have to do it. 

Which is kind of like how I feel about checking the expiration dates on the milk in the fridge at work. I don't even drink milk, but I always find myself looking at the dates because someone left a carton of half-and-half in there for like three months once and it basically turned into cheese. It smelled so bad when the janitor finally threw it out. We have this new janitorial service now because the old one kept forgetting to empty the recycling bins. Our office manager, Sarah, she's super intense about recycling. She actually dug through the trash once to pull out a plastic fork someone threw away and sent a company-wide email about it. She uses so many exclamation points in her emails, it's exhausting to read. It's like she's yelling at you through the screen. My old roommate used to text like that. Every single message was urgent. "We're out of paper towels!!!" Like, okay man, I'll pick some up on my way home, it's not an emergency. He ended up moving out to go to grad school in Chicago. Chicago winters are brutal, I don't know how people deal with the wind coming off the lake. I visited him once in January and my face actually went numb walking from the train station...

Uh, sorry. What were we talking about? The feeling responsible thing? Yeah, no, I don't really think that's it. It's just the anxiety, you know? I just have to do the routine.

doctor.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

target_item.name: Compulsions
target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is that I’m losing hours to rechecking things—my dressing supplies, door locks, file dimensions, revision notes—because I don’t feel allowed to move on until I’ve gone through the same routine enough times that the anxiety drops.

patient.answer:

I'm an engineer, so I'm looking at schematics all day, and we actually just switched to this new project management software last month. It's completely terrible. target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is that I’m losing hours to rechecking things—my dressing supplies, door locks, file dimensions, revision notes—because I don’t feel allowed to move on until I’ve gone through the same routine enough times that the anxiety drops.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the checking routines (compulsions) are performed to prevent feeling responsible/guilty if something bad happens, which directly relates to the purpose of the compulsions (preventing distress/anxiety).

patient.answer:
I mean, maybe? It's not so much about the feeling of responsibility, it's just... I can't stop. What brings me in is that I'm losing hours to rechecking things. Like my dressing supplies for that scrape, the door locks, file dimensions at work, revision notes... I just don't feel allowed to move on until I've gone through the same routine enough times that the anxiety drops. 

Speaking of door locks, my apartment building just installed these new smart locks on all the exterior doors. You have to use an app on your phone to get in now, which is so annoying if your battery dies. And my phone battery is always dying because I have this older iPhone. Apple totally throttles the batteries on older models to force you to upgrade, I swear. I was reading this huge thread on Reddit about it the other night when I couldn't sleep. There's this whole community of people who refuse to upgrade and they just keep replacing the batteries themselves using these tiny little screwdrivers you can buy online. I actually ordered a kit, but when it arrived, the screwdrivers were magnetized, which is supposedly really bad for the logic board. I don't know if that's true, but I didn't want to risk bricking my phone. My buddy Steve bricked his phone once trying to jailbreak it so he could get free games, and he had to go to the Apple Store and pretend he didn't know what happened. The Genius Bar guy totally knew, though. They always know. 

But, uh... wait. What did you ask me? Oh, right, about preventing myself from feeling responsible. I don't know, I just... I just have to do the routine until the anxiety goes away. That's the only way I can explain it.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's checking routines are driven by a fear of being responsible for harm to others
doctor.question: Do you think your checking routines are a way to cope with the fear of being responsible if someone gets hurt because of one of your mistakes?

target_item.reason: The doctor is repeatedly asking variations of the same question (whether the checking routines are to cope with fear of responsibility/guilt for causing harm). The patient has already provided their manifestation for S066 (Compulsions) in response to the previous question and there are no other symptom profile items directly addressing the specific underlying motivation of 'fear of responsibility/guilt' beyond what has already been discussed in Obsessions and Compulsions.

patient.answer:
I don't think it's about coping with the fear of being responsible, really. I just... I don't know, I just don't want anyone to get hurt, so I check. It's not like a conscious thought of "oh, I'll be blamed for this." It's more just this overwhelming feeling that I have to do it. 

Like when I was checking the CAD files yesterday. I had to go through every single layer, even the ones that were just reference lines. Which is so tedious because the software we use is incredibly slow. We're still using this ancient version of AutoCAD from like 2018 because the company doesn't want to pay for the subscription model. They switched to that a few years ago and it made everyone so mad. My boss, Dave, he actually wrote this huge, angry email to their customer support, as if that was going to change their entire corporate business model. Dave is always doing stuff like that. He got into a screaming match with the barista at Starbucks last week because they put whole milk in his latte instead of oat milk. He's super lactose intolerant, to be fair, but still. You don't have to yell at a teenager making minimum wage. I always tip them extra when he does that. I usually use the app to tip, though, because who carries cash anymore? I tried to use a twenty-dollar bill at a food truck the other day and the guy looked at me like I handed him a live grenade. He had this little Square reader plugged into his iPad, but the screen was completely shattered. I don't know how he could even read the orders...

Sorry, I'm doing it again. What was the question? Something about coping with fear? Yeah, I don't really know. I just check because I have to.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's checking routines are driven by a fear of being responsible for harm to others
doctor.question: Do you think your checking routines are mostly about avoiding the feeling of being at fault if something bad happens to someone else?

target_item.reason: The doctor is repeatedly asking if the checking routines are a way to avoid feeling guilty, responsible, or at fault if something bad happens to someone else. This is exploring the specific motivation behind the compulsions (avoidance of guilt/responsibility), which is not explicitly covered in the patient's symptom profile (which only mentions checking until the anxiety drops).

patient.answer:
At fault? I mean, I'm not really thinking about who gets the blame, honestly. I just don't want anything bad to happen. 

Speaking of being at fault, though, my car insurance premium just went up even though I totally wasn't at fault for this fender bender I had last month. This guy in a Prius just backed right into me in the grocery store parking lot. It was the Trader Joe's over on 5th, and their parking lot is an absolute nightmare. They always build them way too small on purpose, I swear. My buddy works in urban planning and he says it's a known psychological trick to make the store seem more exclusive or busy, which is just brilliant but so annoying when you're just trying to buy some frozen potstickers. 

But anyway, the guy tried to say I was in his blind spot. Which is ridiculous because I was completely stationary. Thank god I had a dashcam installed. I bought this really nice Garmin one off Amazon during Prime Day last year. Prime Day deals used to be so good, but now it's just a bunch of cheap drop-shipped electronics with weird brand names in all caps. You really have to use those price tracker extensions on your browser to see if you're actually getting a deal, otherwise they just mark up the base price and pretend it's on sale. I actually wrote a little Python script to track prices for me, since it's easier than relying on third-party extensions that probably just sell your data anyway. Data privacy is basically dead at this point, every single app tracks your location even when you tell it not to...

Wait, sorry. I'm rambling again. What did you ask me? About being at fault? Yeah, I don't really think about the blame part of it. I just get stuck doing the checks until my brain finally lets me move on.

inference.note: F42.0 was ruled out as the patient's symptoms are more focused on checking and preventing harm rather than a broad range of obsessive-compulsive symptoms

patient.answer:
I don't think it's about preventing myself from feeling responsible. I'm not really sitting there thinking about the consequences like that. It's just... I have to do it. 

Which is kind of like how I feel about checking the expiration dates on the milk in the fridge at work. I don't even drink milk, but I always find myself looking at the dates because someone left a carton of half-and-half in there for like three months once and it basically turned into cheese. It smelled so bad when the janitor finally threw it out. We have this new janitorial service now because the old one kept forgetting to empty the recycling bins. Our office manager, Sarah, she's super intense about recycling. She actually dug through the trash once to pull out a plastic fork someone threw away and sent a company-wide email about it. She uses so many exclamation points in her emails, it's exhausting to read. It's like she's yelling at you through the screen. My old roommate used to text like that. Every single message was urgent. "We're out of paper towels!!!" Like, okay man, I'll pick some up on my way home, it's not an emergency. He ended up moving out to go to grad school in Chicago. Chicago winters are brutal, I don't know how people deal with the wind coming off the lake. I visited him once in January and my face actually went numb walking from the train station...

Uh, sorry. What were we talking about? The feeling responsible thing? Yeah, no, I don't really think that's it. It's just the anxiety, you know? I just have to do the routine.
